title: Ethics, communication and palliative care
summary: Ethics, communication and palliative care in the ICU: breaking bad news (SPIKES), family meetings and shared decisions, Indian law on withholding and withdrawing treatment (Common Cause 2018/2023), palliative symptom care and compassionate extubation, the organ donation request, and documentation and medico-legal practice.

topics.title: Breaking bad news (SPIKES)
topics.summary: A six-step structure for giving serious news to patients and families in the ICU, with language that works in Indian settings.

definition.text: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions (Empathy), Strategy and Summary. It structures the conversation so that information is given at the family's pace and emotions are acknowledged before plans are discussed.

steps.title: Setting
steps.detail: Private room, sit down, phones silenced, nurse present, key family decision-makers invited; interpreter if needed (not a child relative).

steps.title: Perception
steps.detail: Ask what they already understand: 'What have the doctors told you so far?'

steps.title: Invitation
steps.detail: Ask how much detail they want and who should receive information.

steps.title: Knowledge
steps.detail: Warning shot ('I am afraid I have serious news'), then plain language in short chunks; avoid jargon and euphemisms; pause.

steps.title: Emotions
steps.detail: Name and acknowledge emotion ('I can see this is a shock'); allow silence; respond with empathy before giving more facts.

steps.title: Strategy and summary
steps.detail: Summarise, check understanding, agree the next step and time of the next update; document the conversation.

tables.title: Useful phrases
rows: 'There is nothing more we can do.'
'We will always care for him; the question is which treatments will help.'
'Do you want us to do everything?'
'What would she say about these treatments if she could speak to us?'
'Stopping treatments that are not helping, while continuing comfort care'
'He is very sick and could die in the next few days despite everything we are doing.'

redFlags.text: Serious news delivered by phone or in a corridor by a junior doctor without preparation - arrange a structured meeting as soon as possible.

pitfalls.text: Giving statistics and options before checking understanding and emotion.
Using medical jargon ('multi-organ dysfunction', 'poor prognosis') without explanation.

pearls.text: Silence after the news is a tool, not a failure - wait for the family to speak.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Families of ICU patients have high rates of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress; how information is given affects these outcomes and trust.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- SPIKES protocol [Baile 2000].
- SCCM family-centred care guidelines [Davidson 2017]; dying in ICU review [Cook 2014].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Disclosure to the patient versus family-mediated disclosure, common in Indian culture.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Decisions in India are usually family-centred; identify the main decision-makers early, but respect a capable patient's own wishes.
- Speak in the family's language; hospital interpreters or trained counsellors are better than relatives translating.

topics.title: Family meetings and shared decision-making
topics.summary: Running a structured family conference (VALUE), handling disagreement and potentially inappropriate treatment requests.

definition.text: A planned family conference within 24-72 h of ICU admission, and whenever the prognosis changes, improves family outcomes. VALUE: Value what the family says, Acknowledge emotions, Listen, Understand the patient as a person, Elicit questions.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.detail: Agree the medical view among the team first (consultant-led); review prognosis, options and the patient's known values; invite nurse and social worker or counsellor.

steps.title: Open
steps.detail: Introductions; purpose of the meeting; ask what they understand.

steps.title: Inform
steps.detail: Clinical update in plain language; honest prognosis including uncertainty (time-limited trial if uncertain).

steps.title: Explore values
steps.detail: 'What kind of person is he? What mattered most to him?' - substituted judgement, not 'what do you want'.

steps.title: Recommend
steps.detail: Make a clear medical recommendation; share the decision; do not ask families to decide alone on withdrawal.

steps.title: Close and document
steps.detail: Summarise, set a review time, document attendees, information, decisions and the patient's goals.

steps.title: Disagreement
steps.detail: Time-limited trial, second opinion, ethics committee or palliative care input; for persistent requests for treatment the team considers inappropriate, use a fair process (ATS multisociety policy).

redFlags.text: Family conflict escalating to threats or violence - involve senior administration and security early; never negotiate alone at the bedside.

pitfalls.text: Presenting a menu of interventions without a recommendation.
Multiple doctors giving inconsistent messages - one consultant voice.

pearls.text: Time-limited trials ('we will try full treatment for 3-5 days and then review together against agreed goals') reduce conflict when prognosis is uncertain.

Meet family: understanding → update → patient's values

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Surrogate decision-makers carry heavy psychological burden; structured, empathetic conferences with more family speaking time reduce PTSD, anxiety and depression in relatives.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- VALUE RCT: proactive conference + brochure reduced PTSD symptoms in relatives at 90 days [Lautrette 2007].
- SCCM 2017 family-centred care [Davidson 2017]; ATS/ESICM/SCCM policy on potentially inappropriate treatments [Bosslet 2015].
- ISCCM 2012 ethical position statement [Chawla 2012].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Who decides when family and team disagree; role of courts versus institutional processes.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Financial burden is a major factor in Indian ICU decisions; discuss costs openly and sensitively, but separately from prognosis.
- ISCCM recommends shared decision-making with the family as the norm; extended families may need a single spokesperson.

topics.title: Withholding and withdrawing treatment in India (law and process)
topics.summary: The legal basis after Common Cause 2018 and the 2023 modification, DNAR, the two-medical-board process and ISCCM guidance.

definition.text: The Supreme Court (Common Cause v Union of India, 2018) recognised the right to die with dignity under Article 21, permitting withholding and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (passive euthanasia) and advance directives. In January 2023 the Court simplified the procedure. Active euthanasia remains illegal.

steps.title: Establish futility or the patient's wish
steps.detail: Terminal illness or irreversible condition with no reasonable hope of recovery, or a capable patient refusing treatment, or a valid advance directive.

steps.title: Capable patient
steps.detail: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment including life support; document the capacity assessment and informed refusal.

steps.title: Primary Medical Board
steps.detail: Hospital board of the treating physician and at least two subject experts with ≥ 5 years experience; decision within 48 h (2023 modification).

steps.title: Secondary Medical Board
steps.detail: Hospital board including a registered medical practitioner nominated by the district Chief Medical Officer and at least two subject experts (≥ 5 years); decision within 48 h; the JMFC is informed.

steps.title: Family consent
steps.detail: Consent of the next of kin / guardian recorded; if the board refuses, family may approach the High Court.

steps.title: DNAR / limitation orders
steps.detail: Withholding CPR or escalation (DNAR, 'allow natural death') is a medical decision taken with the family, documented with reasons and reviewed; it does not mean withdrawing other care.

steps.title: Implement compassionately
steps.detail: Continue comfort care, symptom control and family support; withdraw treatments in a planned sequence (see palliative-symptom-care).

tables.title: Key legal points (India)
rows: Lawful following the Common Cause procedure
Valid; signed before 2 witnesses and attested by notary or gazetted officer (2023)
Primary and secondary boards, each within 48 h; JMFC informed
tables.caption: Summary for clinicians, not legal advice; check hospital policy and legal counsel.

redFlags.text: Withdrawing life support without documented board decisions and family consent exposes the team to legal risk - follow the process.

pitfalls.text: Equating DNAR with 'no treatment' - patients with DNAR orders still receive all appropriate non-CPR care.
'Discharge against medical advice' used as a substitute for an honest end-of-life plan.

pearls.text: Withholding and withdrawing are ethically equivalent (ISCCM) - starting a time-limited trial does not oblige indefinite continuation.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Not applicable - ethical and legal framework.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Common Cause judgment 2018 and 2023 modification [Supreme Court 2018; Supreme Court 2023].
- ISCCM 2012 ethical position statement [Chawla 2012]; ISCCM/IAPC 2024 [Kapadia 2024].
- ACCM end-of-life recommendations [Truog 2008].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Practical feasibility of medical boards in smaller hospitals; withdrawal of artificial nutrition; absence of specific legislation.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Many Indian ICUs still avoid formal withdrawal and rely on DAMA/LAMA discharge; ISCCM/IAPC advocate open, documented end-of-life decisions.
- Keep a hospital SOP and template forms for medical board decisions; check state-level notifications for CMO nominee panels.

topics.title: Palliative symptom care and compassionate extubation
topics.summary: Comfort-focused care at the end of life: pain, breathlessness, agitation and secretions, and how to withdraw ventilation humanely.

definition.text: When goals change to comfort, treat symptoms proactively and stop interventions that do not add comfort. Opioids and sedatives are titrated to relieve distress; the principle of double effect permits this even if death may be hastened.

steps.title: Assess symptoms
steps.detail: Pain (CPOT/BPS), breathlessness (respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, grimacing), agitation, secretions; repeat at least hourly during withdrawal.

steps.title: Stop non-beneficial interventions
steps.detail: Routine bloods, imaging, monitoring alarms, vasopressors, RRT, NG feeding that adds no comfort; keep mouth care, positioning and skin care.

steps.title: Pain and breathlessness
steps.detail: Opioid (morphine or fentanyl) bolus and infusion titrated to comfort; fan and positioning.

steps.title: Anxiety and agitation
steps.detail: Midazolam boluses/infusion; exclude urinary retention and pain.

steps.title: Secretions
steps.detail: Reposition; glycopyrronium or hyoscine butylbromide; gentle oral suction; explain to family.

steps.title: Compassionate extubation
steps.detail: Prepare family; premedicate (opioid ± midazolam) before extubation; stop neuromuscular blockers well before (must have worn off); reduce FiO₂/support then extubate to air or low-flow oxygen; treat distress immediately.

steps.title: After death
steps.detail: Allow family time and rituals; bereavement support; complete death certification.

doseCards.dose: 1-2 mg IV (2.5-5 mg SC) as needed; infusion 0.5-2 mg/h
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg opioid-naive: morphine 2 mg IV before extubation, then 1 mg/h infusion with 2 mg boluses for respiratory distress.
doseCards.verify: Starting doses per local palliative protocol.

20 mg every 4 h as needed (max 120 mg/24 h)

redFlags.text: Patient still paralysed with neuromuscular blockers when ventilation is withdrawn - unacceptable; stop NMB and confirm recovery first.

pitfalls.text: Giving large sedative doses with the stated aim of hastening death - document intent as symptom relief and titrate to symptoms.
Leaving monitors alarming at the bedside during dying.

pearls.text: Ask the family about religious and cultural rituals (prayers, Ganga jal, last rites) and accommodate them in the ICU.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Dyspnoea results from mismatch between respiratory drive and achieved ventilation; opioids reduce the perception of breathlessness and respiratory drive. Secretions pool in the oropharynx when swallowing and cough fail.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ACCM end-of-life care recommendations [Truog 2008].
- NICE NG31 care of dying adults [NICE 2015]; review of dying in ICU [Cook 2014].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Terminal extubation versus terminal weaning; palliative sedation depth.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Morphine access in India is limited by NDPS regulations although simplified since 2014 amendments; ensure the hospital holds a licence and stock (recognised medical institution status).
- Palliative care teams are available in larger centres; ISCCM/IAPC encourage integration with ICU.

topics.title: Organ donation: the request conversation
topics.summary: Identifying potential donors, the mandated request in India, decoupling the request from news of death, and working with transplant coordinators.

definition.text: The THOA amendment (2011) and Rules 2014 require hospitals to ask relatives of a potential brain-stem-dead donor about organ donation and to inform the transplant coordinator. Brain-stem death certification is covered in the raised-icp-neurotrauma-brain-death module.

steps.title: Identify early
steps.detail: Severe brain injury with GCS 3 and absent brainstem reflexes, or planned withdrawal - notify the transplant coordinator (NOTTO/ROTTO/SOTTO network) early.

steps.title: Decouple
steps.detail: Explain death (brain-stem death) first; allow the family to understand it; make the donation request in a separate conversation.

steps.title: Who asks
steps.detail: A trained requester, ideally with the transplant coordinator, in a private setting.

steps.title: Content
steps.detail: Donation is an option and a gift; it is voluntary; no payment; funeral and body appearance not affected; religious views respected.

steps.title: Consent and documentation
steps.detail: Written consent from the person lawfully in possession of the body on the prescribed form; medico-legal cases need police/forensic clearance.

steps.title: Donor management
steps.detail: Continue organ-supportive care (MAP, fluids, temperature, endocrine) after consent - see raised-icp module.

redFlags.text: Raising donation before the family has understood that the patient has died (or will die) - risks distrust and refusal.

pitfalls.text: Not informing the coordinator because 'the family will refuse' - the law requires the request.

pearls.text: Families who decline should still receive full support - the request is an offer, not an obligation.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Not applicable - communication and legal process. Brain-stem death causes haemodynamic, endocrine and temperature instability needing active donor management.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act and Rules 2014 [MoHFW 2014].
- Family-centred communication principles [Davidson 2017].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Donation after circulatory death (DCD) - limited practice in India; 'opt-out' systems.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Deceased donation rates in India are low (< 1 per million population nationally, higher in Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Kerala, Maharashtra); trained ICU requesters and coordinators raise consent rates.
- Medico-legal (road traffic) cases form many potential donors; arrange post-mortem coordination early.

topics.title: Consent, capacity, documentation and medico-legal practice
topics.summary: Informed consent in ICU, capacity and surrogate decisions, medico-legal cases, records, and LAMA/DAMA discharge.

definition.text: Good ICU documentation records what was found, what was decided, why, and who was informed. Indian regulations require indoor records to be kept for at least 3 years and provided to the patient or authorised representative within 72 h of a request.

steps.title: Consent
steps.detail: Informed consent for procedures and high-risk treatment: nature, benefits, risks, alternatives, in the patient's language; emergency treatment can proceed without consent when delay would endanger life (document why).

steps.title: Capacity
steps.detail: Assess decision-specific capacity (understand, retain, weigh, communicate); if absent, involve the legally appropriate surrogate and act in the patient's best interests.

steps.title: Daily notes
steps.detail: Time-stamped entries with problems, plan, discussions with family (who, what was said), and consultant review.

steps.title: Medico-legal cases
steps.detail: Trauma, poisoning, burns, assault, suspicious deaths: register as MLC, inform police, preserve samples (gastric lavage, blood, clothing) with chain of custody.

steps.title: LAMA/DAMA
steps.detail: Explain risks, offer alternatives, document capacity, the information given and signatures of patient/relative and witness; give a discharge summary.

steps.title: Records access
steps.detail: Provide copies within 72 h when requested by patient or authorised representative; maintain confidentiality.

redFlags.text: Altering or adding to notes after an adverse event without dating them as late entries - unethical and legally damaging.

pitfalls.text: Consent forms signed without a documented discussion.
Not documenting family meetings and limitation decisions.

pearls.text: Document the reasoning ('because...') behind major decisions; it protects the patient's interests and the team.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Not applicable - professional and legal framework.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Indian Medical Council Regulations 2002 on records and conduct [MCI 2002].
- ISCCM 2012 statement on decision-making and documentation [Chawla 2012].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Electronic records and audit trails; role of the Consumer Protection Act in ICU litigation.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- The National Medical Commission now regulates professional conduct; the 2002 MCI regulations remain the widely cited standard - check the current NMC regulations.
- Use standard MLC registers and inform the police station as per state rules; death certificates (MCCD) must record the underlying cause.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.indications: Pain and breathlessness at the end of life
drugs.adultDose: Opioid-naive: 1-2 mg IV or 2.5-5 mg SC as needed (every 1-2 h); infusion 0.5-2 mg/h IV/SC titrated to comfort. Patients already on opioids: continue and increase by 25-50% for uncontrolled symptoms.
drugs.preparationIndia: 10 mg/mL and 15 mg/mL ampoules (NDPS licensing required; availability restricted in some hospitals).
drugs.renalHepatic: Active metabolites accumulate in AKI/CKD - use smaller doses, longer intervals or fentanyl.
drugs.cautions: Titrate to symptoms, not to a time of death; document intent (comfort).
drugs.verify: Starting doses are common palliative practice rather than guideline-fixed; confirm with local palliative formulary.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.indications: Anxiety, distress, agitation and palliative sedation at the end of life; seizures
drugs.adultDose: 1-2 mg IV or 2.5-5 mg SC as needed; infusion 0.5-2 mg/h IV/SC titrated to comfort.
drugs.renalHepatic: Accumulates in renal and hepatic failure.
drugs.cautions: Combine with opioid for distressing breathlessness only when anxiety is prominent.
drugs.verify: Doses from palliative practice; confirm locally.

drugs.name: Glycopyrronium (glycopyrrolate)
drugs.adultDose: 200 mcg SC/IV every 4-6 h as needed (maximum about 1.2 mg/24 h).
drugs.cautions: Dry mouth, urinary retention; best given early; reassure families that the noise is rarely distressing to the patient.
drugs.verify: Dose from palliative formularies (NICE NG31 lists drug classes, not doses).

drugs.name: Hyoscine butylbromide
drugs.adultDose: 20 mg SC/IV every 4 h as needed (maximum 120 mg/24 h).
drugs.verify: Dose from palliative formularies; confirm locally.
